Yogurt is a fermented milk product made by pasteurizing milk and allowing it to sit, sometimes for a short period of time, until it becomes creamy and tangy.  To make yogurt, milk is first heated over low heat to around 170 degrees Fahrenheit, then it’s cooled to 140 degrees Fahrenheit, and then the milk is cultured with the bacteria lactic acid bacteria in an incubator, which produces the tangy flavor.

There are several varieties of yogurt: strained or unsstrained, Greek or regular, thick or thin.  Strained yogurt has the liquid part of the milk solidified, while the thickened part remains milk.  Greek yogurt is thick, as is regular yogurt, and most people prefer the tangy taste of strained or thick yogurt over the creamier taste of Greek or regular yogurt.  It’s also worth noting that some yogurts have added fruit, nuts, or other ingredients to them.

The main ingredients in yogurt are milk and lactic acid bacteria.  Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) is found in almost all dairy products.  LAB produces lactic acid, which is a kind of acid that makes dairy products go bad, so LAB is useful in keeping dairy products fresh.  Because LAB doesn’t like to grow in very cold places, its growth in yogurt is usually maintained at around 70 degrees Fahrenheit, which is the temperature at which milk is heated.  

It’s also worth noting that a different kind of bacteria, Streptococcus thermophilus, is used for making酸奶（印度酸奶）and sour milk cheeses.
